title: Things that make you age faster and slower: reading 16 epigenetic clocks against the Blueprint stack
summary: Bryan reacts to a study of 16 epigenetic age clocks across many interventions and maps the results to his own protocol. He explains why he stopped rapamycin, keeps metformin, avoids grains, trusts the DunedinPACE clock, and why single clocks and rodent data are unreliable proxies for human longevity.

principles.text: Continuous measurement of real biomarkers and performance indicators converges on the interventions that best slow epigenetic aging.
principles.quote: continuous measurement and optimization for actual biomarkers and performance indicators automatically consolidates the interventions that best slow down epigenetic biological age.

principles.text: He stopped rapamycin because his own labs showed metabolic side effects, and the clock data did not support it.
principles.quote: In September I stopped Rapamycin, based on concerns around its metabolic side-effects observed in my lab results (including increased cholesterol, blood sugar and RHR)

principles.text: He continues metformin, seeing it as a promising longevity intervention: 5 of 16 clocks improved and none worsened.
principles.quote: 5 out of the 16 clocks indicating significant reduction/deceleration in biological age, with no clock indicating the contrary.

principles.text: A green Mediterranean diet slowed aging on the most clocks and is closest to his Blueprint diet; he stays grain-free.
principles.quote: A green mediterranean diet fared best at reducing/slowing down aging as measured by 10 out of 16 aging clocks, this diet is the closest to my Blueprint diet.

principles.text: He tracks biological age with the DunedinPACE clock, which he considers the most reliable and sensitive, especially in healthy people.
principles.quote: I continuously trace my epigenetic biological age using the PACE (DunedinPACE) clock, as discussed this clock is superior in both reliability and sensitivity

principles.text: Rodent lifespan data is a weak predictor of what works in humans; rapamycin is the example.
principles.quote: This further puts to question the validity of rodent data in predicting longevity interventions in humans.
